summary: The HP performs the blood sprinkling service on the kapporet inside the Holy of Holies. Key topics: the physical technique (tilting the hand like a whip, blood aimed toward the kapporet's thickness rather than its surface), the counting formula ('one; one and one; one and two...' up to one and seven) designed to prevent any error during this most critical service, and the biblical derivation showing why Scripture explicitly states both bull and goat counts rather than relying on analogy (analogy is insufficient when kareth penalties are at stake). The HP then exits, swaps bowls, and re-enters for the identical goat's blood service.

learning.ahaMoment: The physical technique of sprinkling encodes spiritual precision - the blood must fly true without landing on the most sacred surface.

learning.learnerQuestion: Where exactly does the High Priest aim when sprinkling blood before the kapporet - at the flat top surface, at the side, or forward in front of it?
learning.coreTension: The Torah says to sprinkle 'before' the kapporet; the precise target surface or direction - top, side, or forward toward it - must be established, as each implies different physical execution of the rite.
learning.coreMove: The Talmud establishes that the HP sprinkles toward the side (face) of the kapporet, not downward onto its flat top surface; the motion is a forward-and-upward flick toward the kapporet's vertical side.

takeaway.text: The High Priest sprinkles toward the side (face) of the kapporet, directing the blood forward toward its vertical surface, not downward onto its flat top.

learning.learningBlocker: Students imagining the physical act of sprinkling may default to thinking of it as a downward sprinkle onto the top surface of the kapporet, like sprinkling water onto a table.

learning.ahaMoment: The formula is a self-monitoring system: every count carries the first sprinkle within it, making omission or repetition impossible as long as he counts correctly.
learning.memoryAnchor: The 'one and...' formula: you can't forget what you never stop counting.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the Mishnah prescribe a precise verbal counting formula (achat, achat v'achat, achat u'shtayim...) for the blood sprinklings, rather than simply counting silently?
learning.coreTension: Counting is a simple task; an elaborate verbal formula seems excessive. But in a high-stress setting where any miscounting could invalidate the service and require repetition, the counting method must be error-proof.
learning.coreMove: The Talmud explains that the verbal counting formula is specifically designed to prevent losing count: by always including the running total in each call, the HP maintains a cumulative count that makes miscounting nearly impossible even under extreme stress.

takeaway.text: The verbal counting formula for kapporet sprinklings is an error-prevention system: each count includes the running total so that even under stress or distraction, the HP cannot lose his place in the sequence.

learning.learningBlocker: Students see the counting formula as a liturgical formality rather than as a practical error-prevention mechanism designed for a high-stakes, high-stress ritual context.

display.title: Goat's Lower Sprinklings Derived from Its Own Verse

learning.ahaMoment: Scripture is more explicit than logic requires because when kareth is at stake, analogy alone is not enough - lives and atonement cannot rest on implication.
learning.memoryAnchor: When kareth is at stake, Scripture speaks directly: no inference is safe enough for Yom Kippur.
learning.learnerQuestion: Is the number of lower sprinklings for the goat's blood service derived purely by analogy with the bull, or does the Torah provide an independent textual basis for the goat's count?
learning.coreTension: Using analogy alone to derive ritual details can be questioned; if the goat's lower sprinkling count were only inferred from the bull, it could theoretically be rejected by those who do not accept the analogy.
learning.coreMove: The Talmud establishes that the goat's lower sprinkling count has independent derivation from its own verse, not only from analogy with the bull; the verse language for the goat parallels that for the bull, providing an independent textual anchor.

takeaway.text: The seven lower sprinklings for the goat blood service in the Holy of Holies are derived from the goat's own verse, not merely by analogy with the bull; both blood services have independent textual grounding for their counts.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume the goat's service is only a copy of the bull's service, derived entirely by analogy; they miss that each has its own independent textual derivation.

learning.ahaMoment: Two entries to the innermost: one for the priesthood's representative (bull), one for the entire nation (goat). The HP serves as messenger for both.

learning.learnerQuestion: How many separate times does the High Priest enter the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur, and why is it more than the simple bull-and-goat count might suggest?
learning.coreTension: There are two blood services (bull and goat) inside the Holy of Holies, suggesting two entries; but the incense service is also performed inside, adding at least one more entry. The exact total matters for understanding the full ritual sequence.
learning.coreMove: The Talmud establishes that the HP enters the Holy of Holies more than twice: once for the incense service, then again for the bull blood, and again for the goat blood - resulting in at least three separate entries.

takeaway.text: The High Priest enters the Holy of Holies more than twice on Yom Kippur: separate entries are required for the incense service, the bull blood, and the goat blood, totaling at least three distinct entries.

learning.learningBlocker: Students count only the two blood services and assume two entries; the incense service is a distinct entry that they overlook when tallying the HP's movements.

rashiTranslations.en: 'Like this, facing me' - like striking with a strap, starting from the shoulders and striking downward.
'He does not sprinkle on the kapporet' - on its top surface, but rather toward its thickness, and the blood did not
touch it. 'When he sprinkles' - the one upward sprinkling, he tilts the back of his hand downward and sprinkles
toward above; and when he sprinkles the seven downward ones, he tilts his hand upward and sprinkles facing
himself, one higher and one
lower than it, and all of them fall to the ground. 'From where'
are these matters derived - that he does not sprinkle on the kapporet those
two sprinklings, one above for the bull, and one
above for the goat, actually on the top of the kapporet
itself. 'It should not need to say below regarding the goat' - it should not
need to say 'and before the kapporet,' which is the below-sprinkling
for the goat, since it is written regarding it, 'and he shall sprinkle it on'
'the kapporet and before the kapporet' - for it is unnecessary,
since in the end it is derived from the bull's below-sprinkling anyway, for
the verse did not specify how many sprinklings, and we derive it
below from the bull's below-sprinkling, regarding which it is written, 'and before'
'the kapporet he shall sprinkle seven times' - and since in the end
it is derived from there, let the verse be silent about it
and let the whole matter of the goat's below-sprinkling be derived
from the bull's below-sprinkling, since they are juxtaposed, as it is written,
'and he shall do with its blood as he did with the blood of the bull.'
Granted, its above-sprinkling was necessary to state explicitly,
since one sprinkling is specified there, as it is written, 'he shall sprinkle it'
'on the kapporet,' and 'it' implies one - but regarding the bull's
above-sprinkling, one was not specified. 'Why then is it stated' -
the below-sprinkling for the goat, in order to juxtapose it with the goat's own
above-sprinkling, and to teach that 'on the kapporet' means like 'before
the kapporet': just as 'before' does not mean actual contact
with the kapporet, since 'before' implies onto the ground,
even though it does not actually touch the kapporet, but rather
means only that he tilts his hand downward.
'On the contrary, it should not need to say above regarding the bull, since it is'
unnecessary - for in the end it is derived below from the goat's
above-sprinkling, where one sprinkling is specified. 'Why then is it stated?'
'To juxtapose' - the bull's 'before' to the bull's own 'on,'
since the term left free comes to teach. 'Just as 'on''
'means actual contact' - since it is written 'on the face of the kapporet,'
so too 'before' means actual contact, such that the blood
touches the thickness of the kapporet. 'Granted, if you say'
'that the goat's below-sprinkling comes to juxtapose it'
with the bull's above-sprinkling as we said, which troubled you as unnecessary,
it is needed for the teaching in the baraita, etc.
'We learned that the goat's above-sprinkling is one' - since 'it'
implies a single one. 'For Scripture need not have said, etc.' -
since here too it spells out both 'he shall sprinkle,' 'on,' and 'before.'
'Each master follows his own locale, etc.' - in R. Meir's locale
they count the general number first and then
the specific, for example 'twenty-one, twenty-
two'; and in R. Yehuda's locale they state the specific
first, 'two and twenty, three and twenty.'
'So that he not err' - so that he has an interval in between
to focus his attention on the count, so that he not err. 'It taught'
regarding the first sprinkling, etc. - and it is written as a chok (statute),
indicating that it is indispensable. 'There were no shofar-boxes for obligatory bird-offerings' -
a shofar-box in which to place coins for one who owes
an obligatory bird-offering (a zav, a zavah, a woman after childbirth, or one
who defiled the Temple), just as there were shofar-boxes for
voluntary offerings, as is taught below in this same passage, and the priests
would take the coins and offer the birds.
'Because of the mixing of obligatory with voluntary offerings' - lest
one shofar-box be mistaken for another, and he offer from

the obligatory box's coins as a voluntary offering, or from the voluntary box's coins as an obligatory one, and it become invalid, since the obligatory offering is one sin-offering and one burnt-offering, while the voluntary offerings are all burnt-offerings, and the procedure for a burnt-offering and a sin-offering are not the same.

'There is not' - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment continues on 55b with Rabbi Yehuda's own position, that documentary labeling on the shofar-boxes is not a reliable safeguard against mixing up the coins.
